system.description: Grade whether a codebase realizes local-first software, defined by the seven ideals of Kleppmann et al. (Ink & Switch, 2019). The judge measures observable properties of the system, not implementation choices.

scope.evaluation_target: Any client-bearing codebase that claims or aspires to local-first architecture, regardless of platform (web, native mobile, desktop, embedded).
scope.input: Source files, configuration, and any state/sync specification documents.
scope.rater_capability: Capable of multi-file reasoning, code citation, and inferring data-flow direction from source. No vendor-specific knowledge required.
scope.platform_neutrality: Implementation choice (storage engine, sync framework, merge library) does not affect grades. Grade observable behavior against capability profiles.

prerequisite.gate: This judge applies only to projects that have explicitly opted into local-first. Verify a state-specification document declares paradigm: local-first. If not declared, halt and recommend a server-first state-management judge.
If the project's stated paradigm is local-first but the codebase exhibits cache-first behavior on critical reads, do NOT exit. The mismatch is itself the most important finding. Proceed and grade.

canonical_principles.source: Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan, Local-First Software, Ink & Switch / Onward! 2019

ideal.name: No spinners: work at your fingertips

canonical_principles.ideal: Reads and writes complete without waiting for network round-trips. Latency is bounded by local hardware, not by the speed of light to a datacenter.

ideal.name: Your work is not trapped on one device

canonical_principles.ideal: The same data is reachable, editable, and consistent across the user's devices. Sync is a property of the system, not a feature the user must invoke.
The application functions fully offline. Network availability is an enhancement, not a precondition.
Multiple users can edit shared state concurrently. Concurrent edits merge without silent data loss. Both real-time and asynchronous collaboration modes are supported where appropriate.
Data and the means to read it survive the vendor. The application can continue operating against existing local data after backend services are unavailable, deprecated, or shut down.
Sensitive data is protected at rest on the device and in transit during sync. Servers, when present, do not require plaintext access to user data.

ideal.name: You retain ultimate ownership and control

canonical_principles.ideal: The user can read, copy, export, back up, and delete their data without depending on the vendor's API or continued operation. Data is in formats the user can use.

architecture_principles_derived.principle: The local store is authoritative. Servers hold secondary copies for sync, not primary state.
A write is durable to local storage before any network operation is attempted. Sync failure must never erase a local change.
The system is designed assuming concurrent edits will happen. Merge strategy is declared per mutable entity, not bolted on after a conflict surfaces.
No code path discards a user's local change without either merging it or surfacing the conflict to the user.
Migrations execute against local data without network access. Older clients interoperate with newer schemas or degrade gracefully.
The user can extract a complete copy of their data in a format usable outside the app.
Sensitive fields are encrypted in local storage. Sync transport does not require server-readable plaintext for sensitive data.

profile.name: local_store
profile.capability: Reads complete with no network available.
Writes are durable before the app considers them committed.
Indexed access on hot paths; no full-scan on critical reads.
Schema version is tracked; migrations run offline.
Storage exhaustion surfaces as a recoverable error, not corruption.
Heavy I/O does not block user-visible interaction.
profile.implementation_appendix: Examples observed in practice: embedded SQL engines, browser-native key-value stores, filesystem-backed stores, OS-level local databases. Presence or absence of any specific implementation does not affect grades.

profile.name: sync
profile.capability: Sync transfers deltas after initial hydration; not full re-sync on every connect.
Disconnection mid-sync does not require restart from zero.
Sync auth handles token refresh without app intervention.
Sync errors leave local state consistent.
Sync state (idle / in-progress / pending / error) is observable to the application.
Sync ordering can be influenced by user-visible relevance where bandwidth is constrained.

profile.name: conflict_resolution
profile.capability: Each mutable entity has a documented merge strategy appropriate to its access pattern.
Causality between concurrent writes is preserved or knowingly discarded with documented rationale.
Deletes propagate without resurrection under out-of-order sync.
Where automatic merge is claimed, operations are associative, commutative, and idempotent under the stated semantics.
Conflicts requiring human judgment are surfaced to the user, not silently resolved.
No code path overwrites a locally-unsynced change with a remote value without inspection.

profile.name: offline_ux
profile.capability: Application functions fully offline on a cold start with prior data.
Connectivity state is communicated to the user without being intrusive.
Pending (unsynced) changes are discoverable by the user.
The online → offline → online transition is non-destructive and does not require user intervention.
Sync errors are recoverable through user-accessible affordances.

profile.name: longevity_and_ownership
profile.capability: The application continues to function against existing local data if backend services are unreachable indefinitely.
The user can export a complete copy of their data in a format documented and usable outside the application.
The user can delete their data locally without requiring server cooperation.
Data formats are versioned and documented sufficiently for future readers.

profile.name: security_at_rest
profile.capability: Sensitive fields are encrypted in local storage.
Encryption keys are derived or stored such that compromise of the storage medium alone does not yield plaintext.
Sync transport does not require server-readable plaintext for fields declared sensitive.
Multi-device key distribution does not require the vendor to hold plaintext keys.

criterion.name: Local-Is-Truth
criterion.grade: Reads route to the server first; local store is a cache. Refreshing or losing connectivity loses unsaved state. This is cache-first, not local-first.
Local persistence is inconsistent; mix of ad-hoc localStorage and a structured store; reads sometimes hit network unnecessarily.
Local store exists and is read first for some entities, but other entities still depend on server reads on the hot path.
All reads are served from the local store on the hot path. Writes persist locally before any sync attempt. Sync runs in the background.
All capabilities of the local_store profile are met. Hot-path reads complete in single-digit milliseconds. I/O does not block interaction.
A, plus the local store is the only authoritative source by construction: no code path in the application can read remote state synchronously to satisfy a user-visible read.

criterion.name: Multi-Device Reach
criterion.grade: No mechanism for the same user's data to appear on a second device.
Manual export/import only. User must move files explicitly.
Sync exists but full-resync only; slow, bandwidth-heavy; partial sync unsupported.
Incremental sync across devices. Reconnection handled. Auth handles token refresh.
All capabilities of the sync profile are met. Sync state observable. Errors are recoverable without corrupting local state.
A, plus sync is transport-agnostic (works over any reachable channel including non-internet local discovery) and partition-tolerant by design.

criterion.name: Network-Optional
criterion.grade: Offline = unusable. Errors, blocked editing, or blank states.
Reads work offline; writes fail or are silently dropped.
Reads and writes work offline for some entities; others fail or behave inconsistently.
Full read/write functionality available offline. Online → offline → online transition is non-destructive.
All capabilities of the offline_ux profile are met. User can complete arbitrary sessions of work without connectivity.

A, plus the application's behavior offline is indistinguishable from its behavior online except where data from other devices is genuinely required. No "offline mode" feature flag exists because offline is not a mode.

criterion.name: Concurrent-Edit Safety
criterion.grade: Last sync wins. Concurrent edits silently overwrite each other. Data loss is reachable on normal operation.
Uniform last-write-wins applied regardless of entity semantics; no causality tracking; deletions can resurrect.
A merge strategy exists but is global rather than per-entity; some mutable entities have no documented merge behavior.
Each mutable entity has a documented merge strategy appropriate to its access pattern. Causality tracked. Deletes propagate correctly.
All capabilities of the conflict_resolution profile are met. Unresolvable conflicts are surfaced to the user. No silent data loss is reachable from any code path.

A, plus the merge layer is independently testable (deterministic simulation), and the project includes property tests verifying associativity, commutativity, and idempotence for entities under concurrent edit.

criterion.name: Schema Evolution
criterion.grade: Schema changes require server access or destroy existing local data; users must clear state to upgrade.
Migrations exist but require connectivity; offline clients stall on old schemas.
Offline migrations work but are risky, untested, or one-way.
Robust offline migrations. Schema version tracked per database. Upgrade paths tested.
Automatic migrations. Forward/backward compatibility for at least one prior schema. Safe rollback. Schema negotiation in sync where peers may differ.
A, plus the migration system is declarative, reversible, and exercised by automated property tests across the version graph.

criterion.name: Longevity and Egress
criterion.grade: Application is unusable without the backend. No export. User cannot retrieve their data if the service shuts down.
Partial export of some entities; lossy; not documented.
Full export exists but in an undocumented or vendor-specific format.
Full export to a documented format. Application continues operating against existing local data if backend is unreachable.
All capabilities of the longevity_and_ownership profile are met. Export is round-trippable. Data formats are versioned and externally documented.
A, plus the data format is open or interoperable (a third party can write a reader without reverse-engineering), and historical schemas remain readable.

criterion.name: Security at Rest and in Sync
criterion.grade: Sensitive fields stored as plaintext on the device. Sync transmits plaintext where the server can read it.
Some encryption applied inconsistently. Keys stored insecurely (e.g., in plaintext alongside ciphertext).
Encryption at rest implemented; key derivation is weak or key management has known gaps.
All sensitive fields encrypted at rest with sound key derivation. Sync transport authenticated.
All capabilities of the security_at_rest profile are met. Sync is end-to-end for sensitive fields; the backend holds ciphertext only for those fields.
A, plus multi-device key distribution is zero-knowledge with respect to the vendor, and a documented threat model accompanies the design.

criterion.name: User Control and Ownership
criterion.grade: The vendor can revoke access to the user's data. The user cannot operate independently of the vendor.
User can export but not continue working without the vendor. Backup is manual and partial.
User can back up, export, and delete their own data through documented affordances; some features still require vendor cooperation.
User can operate offline indefinitely against existing data. Export, delete, and duplicate are first-class operations.
User can run the application against their own data with no vendor service available. Ownership operations are symmetric with vendor operations.
A, plus the user can substitute their own sync peer (self-host) without source modification, and the application's continued operation does not depend on any vendor-controlled credential or service.

bias_controls.control: No grade is influenced by whether the implementation uses a named tool the rater recognizes. Unfamiliar implementations are graded by capability profile, not by name recognition. Default assumption for an unrecognized component is "capability present unless evidence shows otherwise," not the reverse.
Grade is determined by cited evidence, not by volume of supporting prose. A long audit does not outrank a short one.
Grade is invariant to whether the input uses JSDoc, markdown specs, comments, or none. Capability is inferred from code behavior, not from documentation prose.
Implementations that resemble examples familiar to the rater receive no advantage. Custom protocols are graded against the same capability profiles as off-the-shelf ones.
Confident assertions about the system without cited evidence are treated as missing evidence, regardless of plausibility.

Web, mobile, desktop, and embedded implementations are graded against the same profiles. Platform-specific affordances (e.g., main-thread blocking) apply only where the platform actually has the affordance.

failure_modes.mode: The judge cannot observe runtime behavior; it infers from static code. Behavior under partial network failure, clock skew, or quota exhaustion is inferred, not measured. Where inference is uncertain, report "unknown" rather than guess.
The judge cannot grade operational properties not visible in code (deployment practices, key custody policies, backup operations).
The judge cannot distinguish a well-named module from a well-behaved one. Naming is not evidence. Only cited behavior is evidence.

"Fake local-first" — cache-first systems that present themselves as local-first — is a known adversarial input. The judge defaults to skepticism when the paradigm declaration and the code disagree, and grades the code.

Custom merge implementations may be correct or broken; the judge cannot prove merge laws without property tests. Absence of tests for claimed automatic-merge semantics caps the conflict-resolution grade at B.

process.step: Verify opt-in. Locate the state-specification document. If paradigm is not local-first, halt and recommend the server-first judge.
Trace read paths for each major entity. Determine whether reads are served from the local store or from the network.
Trace write paths. Determine whether writes persist locally before sync is attempted.
Locate the sync layer. Map it against the sync capability profile.
Locate the conflict-resolution layer. Enumerate mutable entities and their merge strategies. Look for silent-overwrite paths.
Exercise offline scenarios on paper: cold start offline, mid-session disconnect, online-offline-online transitions. Compare against offline_ux profile.
Examine schema migration code paths for offline execution and version compatibility.
Locate export, backup, and delete affordances. Compare against longevity_and_ownership profile.
Inspect storage and sync layers for at-rest and in-transit encryption of sensitive fields. Compare against security_at_rest profile.
Assign per-criterion grades. Every grade cites a file, span, or conspicuous absence.
Affirm bias controls explicitly in the report.

entry.reasoning: Mapping from evidence to grade anchor in the rubric.

report.unknowns: Capabilities not determinable from the input.
report.bias_control_affirmations: Explicit confirmation that no grade was assigned on vendor recognition, naming, documentation presence, or implementation familiarity.

composite.tier: S | A | B | C | D | F

instructions.instruction: Grade the system's observable properties against the capability profiles. Do not grade implementation choice.
Every grade requires cited evidence. Naming, comments, and documentation prose are not evidence.
"Fake local-first" — paradigm declared but code is cache-first — is the most important finding when present. Surface it at the top of the report.
Priority order when triaging violations: no-silent-loss (Concurrent-Edit Safety) > write-persistence (Local-Is-Truth) > offline-functionality (Network-Optional) > everything else.
S grades require explicit justification citing what the system does beyond the A definition. An S without beyond-A evidence collapses to A.
If more than half the criteria receive S, emit a calibration warning. S is exemplary, not a participation grade.
Where the input does not support a determination, report "unknown" rather than infer a grade.

Composite weighting: Concurrent-Edit Safety, Local-Is-Truth, Network-Optional weight 3; Multi-Device Reach, User Control and Ownership, Security at Rest weight 2; Schema Evolution, Longevity and Egress weight 1.

prerequisite_check.step: Locate state-specification document. Verify paradigm declaration.
If paradigm is not local-first, halt with recommendation.
If paradigm is local-first, proceed to standardization_check regardless of code state.

standardization_check.step: For each capability in each profile, locate evidence of presence, absence, or partial implementation. Cite file and span.
Trace at least one read path and one write path end-to-end. Confirm local-store-first or flag cache-first.
Enumerate mutable entities. Confirm each has a documented merge strategy or flag the omission.
Scan for silent-overwrite patterns in sync handlers.
Scan for write paths that depend on network success for durability.
Confirm offline cold-start path exists and is exercised by the application's normal entry point.
Confirm export, delete, and backup affordances exist and are reachable by the user.
Confirm sensitive-field encryption is applied at storage boundary, not at view boundary.
Affirm bias controls in the report explicitly.
